query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy, raising the temperature to the elevated regime (e.g., 700–900 °C) thermally activates local lattice instabilities that enhance dislocation mobility and incipient amorphous patches, thereby reducing yield strength and elastic modulus while increasing the thermal expansion coefficient compared to room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr with significant intrinsic lattice distortion from the random distribution of elements.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating during mechanical testing to incrementally raise the temperature from room temperature to elevated levels (~700–900 °C) while monitoring stress–strain behavior and thermal expansion.
generation.conditions: Quasi-static tensile or compression tests and simultaneous in situ microstructural characterization conducted at room temperature (baseline) and at high temperatures (700–900 °C) under controlled atmospheres to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and thermally induced modifications in dislocation nucleation and motion (including potential incipient amorphization) that mediate changes in the overall mechanical response.
generation.mechanism: As temperature increases, enhanced atomic vibrations overcome dislocation barriers, leading to modifications in slip system activation and localized lattice instabilities. These changes reduce the elastic modulus and yield strength while simultaneously promoting a higher thermal expansion due to increased atomic spacing and transient, nanoscale disorder.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the room-temperature baseline, at elevated temperatures the alloy is expected to exhibit a noticeable decrease in yield strength and elastic modulus and an increase in the thermal expansion coefficient, with microstructural observations revealing signs of localized lattice instabilities or early-stage amorphization.
generation.baseline: Mechanical and thermal properties measured at room temperature in the homogeneous, BCC-structured HfNbTaTiZr alloy without significant thermal activation of additional deformation mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is anticipated to hold for temperatures up to about 900 °C, below the threshold at which irreversible microstructural degradation (such as precipitation or substantial phase transformation) becomes dominant.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise temperature onset of the thermally activated lattice instabilities and the exact magnitude of changes in mechanical properties; the extent and detectability of any incipient amorphization also require further quantitative investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature tensile (or compression) tests on HfNbTaTiZr specimens using a heating stage integrated with electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction. Measure stress–strain curves, elastic modulus, yield strength, and thermal expansion coefficients across the temperature range from room temperature to 900 °C. Concurrently, capture microstructural changes (e.g., evidence of increased dislocation activity or early amorphous regions) using high-resolution imaging.
measurements: Yield strength and elastic modulus via stress–strain curves
Thermal expansion coefficients via dilatometry or in situ imaging
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/Electron Diffraction) to detect local lattice disorder or amorphization
In situ diffraction patterns to track phase stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, at elevated temperatures (up to 900 °C), the measured yield strength and elastic modulus do not decrease and the thermal expansion coefficient does not increase relative to baseline values, or if no evidence of local lattice instability or incipient amorphous regions is observed through microstructural analyses, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Elastic strain-induced amorphization in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractElastic stability is the basis for understanding structural responses to external stimuli in crystalline solids, including melting, incipient plasticity and fracture. In this work, elastic stability is investigated in a series of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) using in situ mechanical tests and atomic-resolution characterization in transmission electron microscopy. Under tensile loading, the HEA lattices are observed to undergo a sudden loss of ordering as the elastic strain reached ∽ 10%. Such elastic strain-induced amorphization stands in intrinsic contrast to previously reported dislocation-mediated elastic instability and defect accumulation-mediated amorphization, introducing a form of elastic instability. Together with the first principle calculations and atomic-resolution chemical mapping, we identify that the elastic strain-induced amorphization is closely related to the depressed dislocation nucleation due to the local atomic environment inhomogeneity of HEAs. Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries.
